course_name_original: Técnicas de Medida y Tratamiento de Datos en Ingeniería Energética
course_name_en: Measurement Techniques and Data Processing in Energy Engineering
prerequisites: Basic knowledge and competences from undergraduate degrees or equivalent with basic Physics and Mathematics training.
Notions of Thermodynamics, Heat Transfer, and Fluid Mechanics.
Basic knowledge of software for calculations and result representation, such as Microsoft Excel or Matlab.

learning_outcomes.text: Possess and understand knowledge that provides a basis or opportunity to be original in the development and/or application of ideas, often in a research context.

Students should know how to apply acquired knowledge and their problem-solving ability in new or little-known environments within broader (or multidisciplinary) contexts related to their field of study.

Students should be able to integrate knowledge and face the complexity of formulating judgments based on information that, being incomplete or limited, includes reflections on social and ethical responsibilities linked to the application of their knowledge and judgments.
Students should know how to communicate their conclusions and the knowledge and ultimate reasons that support them to specialized and non-specialized audiences clearly and unambiguously.
Students should possess learning skills that allow them to continue studying in a largely self-directed or autonomous way.
The ability to solve problems in new or little-known environments within multidisciplinary contexts related to energy engineering.
Achieving the ability to integrate knowledge to formulate applications for the development of new energy technologies.

The ability of autonomous learning that allows continuing to study through the development of the capacity to search for specialized documentation in cutting-edge scientific-technical literature and its assimilation.
Application of experimentation techniques for measuring variables and testing the operating performance of machines and equipment.
Design, planning, and development of simple experiments for studies on flows and energy transfer.
Acquisition, processing, and analysis of signals in time and frequency domains.
Uncertainty analysis of numerical predictions and experimental measurements in thermal and fluid processes.
Ability to identify, analyze and evaluate the dominant basic phenomena in fluid-mechanical processes and energy transfer and utilization in engineering and industry.
Fundamental analysis of fluid-mechanical and thermal problems of interest in the energy industry, identifying strong and weak variables and evaluating possible simplifying hypotheses.
Know the physical-mathematical models that can be proposed in mass, momentum, and energy transfer processes and the simplifications to be made to solve the governing equations.
Identify, analyze, and evaluate the variables involved in a thermal or fluid process.
Choose the most convenient sensors and measurement equipment in the real study of a fluid-mechanical and/or thermal phenomenon.
Analyze the errors and uncertainties produced in a measurement.
Design experiments through which data of a fluid-mechanical and/or thermal phenomenon can be obtained in the time and frequency domains.
Use computer tools for the acquisition, processing, and analysis of signals in the time and frequency domains.

syllabus_topics: Experiments, variables and measurements in Energy Engineering
Sensors used in the measurement of variables of thermal or fluid processes
Systems for acquisition, processing and analysis of signals in time and frequency domains.
teaching_methods: Virtual Campus activities (reading theoretical fundamentals, solving questionnaires, participating in debate forums, viewing materials)

assessment_methods.method: Practical work (P1) - guided by the professor, written defense required
Practical work (P2) - autonomous, oral defense required

assessment_rules: For the ordinary call, the final grade is calculated as (0.4 x PA) + (0.3 x P1) + (0.3 x P2). No minimum grade is required for individual components. For the extraordinary call, the final grade is calculated as (0.6 x T1) + (0.2 x P1) + (0.2 x P2), where T1 is a theoretical exam and P1 and P2 scores from continuous assessment are kept. For differentiated evaluation, the final grade is calculated as (0.6 x T1) + (0.4 x P1), with P1 being a specific assignment.
